questions.q: In Meridian's architecture, how does the product page get a tent's data to display?
options: It reads the product document directly from MongoDB — no join or reconstruction needed
It queries Neo4j for the product's relationships first
It reads from Cosmos DB's cart container
It joins three separate relational tables at request time
questions.explain: The product page reads straight from MongoDB, since the document already has the shape the page needs.

questions.q: Why does placing an order publish an event instead of writing directly to Neo4j during checkout?
options: So checkout doesn't depend on a fourth system being up, and the two platforms stay decoupled
Neo4j cannot accept writes from application code
Events are required by MongoDB's replication protocol
Cosmos DB blocks direct writes to other databases
questions.explain: A synchronous write to Neo4j during checkout would make the checkout path depend on a fourth system — the event-driven sync job avoids that coupling.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the real relationship between MongoDB, Cosmos DB, and Neo4j in Meridian's architecture?
options: Three independent systems, each owning its own data, kept in sync by events and jobs — not one shared database with three faces
One underlying database exposing three different query languages
MongoDB is the primary store and the other two are read replicas of it
They share a single unified schema enforced across all three platforms
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit: MongoDB doesn't know Neo4j exists, and vice versa — the application layer and sync jobs are what make it look like one architecture.

questions.q: What is a real operational cost of running three data platforms instead of one, per this lesson?
options: Three separate backup strategies, three security surfaces, and a sync job that can fail quietly while checkout keeps working
There is no additional operational cost — more platforms are always strictly easier to run
MongoDB and Cosmos DB cannot both be monitored by the same DBA
Neo4j requires the other two platforms to be shut down during backups
questions.explain: The lesson lists concrete, real costs: separate backups, separate security surfaces, separate monitoring, and the silent-failure risk of a sync job going down.

questions.q: What is the real benefit that this lesson says justifies the added operational cost of polyglot persistence?
options: Each problem is solved by the tool actually built for it, instead of one architecture that fails slowly as every problem worsens at scale
Running three platforms is always cheaper than running one
It eliminates the need for any backups at all
It removes the need for a DBA to monitor the system
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as a real tradeoff: a single 'one database for everything' architecture would fail slowly as each of Meridian's three problems separately worsened with scale.
